name: LEOPARD syndrome (Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines)

clinicalPearls: LEOPARD syndrome, now more often termed Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines, is an autosomal dominant RASopathy that overlaps clinically with Noonan syndrome
The acronym summarises multiple Lentigines, ECG conduction abnormalities, Ocular hypertelorism, Pulmonary stenosis, Abnormalities of the genitalia, Retardation of growth and sensorineural Deafness

Most cases arise from specific missense variants in PTPN11 (encoding the phosphatase SHP-2); unlike the activating variants of Noonan syndrome, these are catalytically impairing and act in a dominant-negative manner
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is more characteristic than in Noonan syndrome and is a major determinant of outcome; pulmonary valve stenosis and conduction abnormalities also occur
The lentigines are numerous small dark macules that appear in childhood, increase with age and spare the mucosae; scattered cafe-au-lait macules are common
Overlap with neurofibromatosis (cafe-au-lait macules) and with other RASopathies can cause diagnostic confusion that is resolved by phenotype and genetic testing
Sensorineural deafness and variable learning difficulty may be present, and growth is often reduced
Management is multidisciplinary, with particular attention to cardiac surveillance (echocardiography and ECG) and hearing assessment
reference.pathophysiology: LEOPARD syndrome belongs to the RASopathies, a group of developmental disorders caused by germline variants that dysregulate the RAS-mitogen-activated protein kinase (RAS-MAPK) signalling pathway. The majority of cases result from heterozygous missense variants in PTPN11, which encodes the protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP-2. The variants responsible for LEOPARD syndrome characteristically reduce catalytic activity and act in a dominant-negative fashion, in contrast to the gain-of-function variants that cause most Noonan syndrome; a minority of cases are due to variants in other pathway genes such as RAF1 and BRAF. Perturbed RAS-MAPK signalling during development gives rise to the characteristic pigmentary lesions, craniofacial features, cardiac malformation and cardiomyopathy, growth restriction, genital anomalies and sensorineural hearing loss. The particular predilection for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy reflects the specific downstream signalling consequences of these variants in the developing and postnatal heart.
additionalDifferentials: Noonan syndrome (allelic, but with activating PTPN11 variants and fewer lentigines)
Neurofibromatosis type 1 (cafe-au-lait macules, neurofibromas and Lisch nodules)
Other RASopathies including cardiofaciocutaneous and Costello syndromes
Carney complex and other lentiginosis syndromes, some with mucosal lentigines
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (mucocutaneous pigmentation, but perioral and gastrointestinal)
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and pulmonary valve stenosis
Audiological assessment for sensorineural hearing loss
Molecular genetic testing of PTPN11 and, if negative, other RASopathy genes such as RAF1 and BRAF
Growth monitoring with assessment of pubertal and genital development
Dermatological review to characterise the lentigines and cafe-au-lait macules
Developmental and cognitive assessment where learning difficulty is suspected
redFlags: Symptoms or signs of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy such as exertional syncope, chest pain or heart failure
Significant conduction abnormality or arrhythmia on ECG
Family history of sudden cardiac death
Severe pulmonary valve stenosis with evidence of right heart strain
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends largely on the cardiac phenotype: many individuals do well with surveillance, but significant or obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy increases the risk of heart failure and sudden cardiac death. Most other features are managed supportively, and life expectancy is often near normal in the absence of severe cardiomyopathy.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the condition as neurofibromatosis because of the cafe-au-lait macules
Assuming the cardiac risk mirrors Noonan syndrome and underestimating the propensity to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Attributing multiple lentigines to benign familial freckling and missing the syndrome
Overlooking sensorineural deafness in a child with pigmentary and cardiac findings
Expecting a standard Noonan interpretation of PTPN11 testing when the causative variants and their functional effect differ
management: There is no curative therapy; management centres on the cardiac phenotype, especially hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Manage hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with beta-blockers and assessment for septal reduction in obstructive disease, and treat significant pulmonary valve stenosis with balloon valvuloplasty
Assess sudden-cardiac-death risk and consider an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, and pace clinically important conduction abnormalities
Provide hearing aids or other audiological support for sensorineural deafness, and monitor growth and pubertal and genital development
Offer dermatological review of the lentigines, with laser therapy where there is cosmetic concern
Undertake regular surveillance with echocardiography, electrocardiography and audiometry
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant PTPN11-related condition with cascade screening of relatives
